sections.h2: How is Missouri property tax assessed?
sections.html:
County assessors set the values, and the percentage applied depends on what the property is used for. Under RSMo 137.115, residential real property is assessed at 19 percent of true value, agricultural land at 12 percent and commercial property at 32 percent. Personal property is generally assessed at one third of its true value as of January 1.

Real property is revalued on a two-year cycle. New assessed values are determined as of January 1 of each odd-numbered year and entered in the assessor's books, and the same values carry into the next even-numbered year, apart from new construction and improvements. The last reassessment year was 2025, so the values on a 2026 bill come from that cycle and the next general reassessment falls in 2027. A county can vote to opt out of the reassessment provisions for its next general reassessment year, so ask your own assessor which schedule applies.

A few protections apply to homeowners. Before the assessor raises a residential parcel's value by more than fifteen percent since the last assessment, apart from new construction, the assessor must make a physical inspection, and a drive-by does not count. The owner has at least thirty days to ask that the inspection include the interior. A taxpayer whose land changes use may also apply to the assessor for reclassification.

sections.h2: When are Missouri property taxes due?
sections.html:
The bill must be paid to the county collector by December 31 each year. The State Tax Commission's guidance says that interest and penalties apply after that date. Collectors may accept credit cards and electronic transfers, and the statute lets a county pass along only the fee it is charged by the card or payment processor.

If you plan to sell in the fall or winter, ask the county collector for the balance on the parcel and for any delinquent amounts from earlier years. Hand that figure to your closing agent before you accept an offer, so nothing about the bill surprises you at the table.

Appealing the value does not require you to pay first, but waiting has consequences. The Commission notes that you may appeal to the county Board of Equalization or the State Tax Commission even when the taxes are unpaid, while unpaid taxes keep collecting interest and penalties.

sections.h2: How do you appeal a Missouri assessment?
sections.html:
Start with the county Board of Equalization, and file by the second Monday in July. That is the deadline the State Tax Commission gives for an assessment appeal at the county level. If the board rules against you, you have thirty days from the date of its decision letter to appeal to the State Tax Commission using the Complaint for Review of Assessment form.

The form can be filed online, emailed to Legal@stc.mo.gov or mailed to State Tax Commission, PO Box 146, Jefferson City, MO 65102-0146. Attach a copy of the tax bill or the board's decision letter and hold the rest of your evidence until the hearing process asks for it. If the property is owned by a corporation, LLC, limited partnership, trust or estate, an attorney must file the appeal or it will be rejected.

There are two situations in which you may go straight to the State Tax Commission:

  • the assessor never notified the current owner of the assessment or an increase, at least thirty days before the county appeal deadline, including cases where the prior owner got the notice;
  • a new owner bought less than thirty days after the county mailed the tax statement.

A stipulation signed with the assessor at the board stage ends the matter, and no further appeal to the Commission is allowed. In charter counties and the City of St. Louis, a computer-generated valuation of residential property puts the burden on the assessor, who must show appraisal findings and at least three comparable sales.

sections.h2: How does paying property tax under protest work?
sections.html:
You pay the full bill to the county collector by December 31, write "paid under protest" on the check, and file a written statement with the collector explaining the grounds. If you dispute the assessed value, the statement must give the fair market value you claim. A payment and statement mailed with a postmark no later than December 31 are treated as timely.

Skipping both the protest and the appeal has a cost. The Commission's guidance says that if taxes were paid without protest and no appeal was filed by the deadline, the law does not let the taxpayer challenge that year's assessment. The owner can still appeal to the Board of Equalization the following year, again by the second Monday in July.

An owner who thinks the value is too high has a short window each year, so mark the July date on the calendar before you list the house.

sections.h2: What relief exists for senior and disabled Missouri owners?
sections.html:
The Missouri Department of Revenue runs the Property Tax Credit Claim, often called the circuit breaker. It gives certain senior citizens and 100 percent disabled individuals a credit for part of the real estate tax or rent paid during the year. The maximum credit is $1,100 for owners who owned and occupied their home and $750 for renters. The actual amount depends on the tax or rent paid and total household income, taxable and nontaxable. A renter in a facility that pays no property tax is not eligible.

Questions about personal property tax go to the county assessor, not to the Department of Revenue. The Department's page lists claim assistance and a PropertyTaxCredit@dor.mo.gov email address for questions about the credit. Owners who are weighing a sale can use those contacts to ask how a move would affect a claim.

sections.h2: What happens if Missouri property tax goes unpaid?
sections.html:
Land with delinquent taxes can be sold at the collector's sale on the fourth Monday in August. RSMo 140.150 requires the collector to mail a first notice to the recorded owner, and to send a second certified notice when the assessed value is above $1,000. Missing the notice does not cancel the debt, and the taxes can still be paid to the collector at any time before the sale.

After a sale, RSMo 140.340 gives the owner, a lienholder, an occupant or anyone with an interest an absolute right to redeem during the next year. The right to redeem continues in a weaker, defeasible form until the buyer acquires the deed. Redemption costs the purchase money and sale costs, interest at the rate on the certificate up to ten percent annually, and later taxes the buyer paid with eight percent interest.

Owners behind on tax who want to sell should ask the county collector for the full payoff, including interest, before the August sale date, since a sold certificate adds costs to every redemption.

faqs.q: What percentage of value does Missouri use for residential property tax?
faqs.a: Residential real property is assessed at 19 percent of true value under RSMo 137.115. Agricultural land is assessed at 12 percent and commercial property at 32 percent.

faqs.q: Which month do I have to file a Missouri assessment appeal?
faqs.a: File with the county Board of Equalization by the second Monday in July. If the board denies the appeal, you have thirty days from the date of its decision letter to appeal to the State Tax Commission.

faqs.q: Can I appeal before paying my property tax?
faqs.a: Yes. The State Tax Commission says you may appeal to the board or the Commission even when the taxes are unpaid. Interest and penalties still build on an unpaid bill after December 31, so many owners pay under protest instead.

faqs.q: Does my Missouri property get revalued every year?
faqs.a: No. New assessed values are set in odd-numbered years and carry into the following even-numbered year, except for new construction and improvements. The most recent reassessment was in 2025, and the next general reassessment is in 2027.

faqs.q: Who qualifies for the Missouri Property Tax Credit?
faqs.a: Certain senior citizens and 100 percent disabled individuals qualify. The credit is capped at $1,100 for owners who owned and occupied their home and $750 for renters, and the amount depends on tax or rent paid and total household income.
